marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q001.takeaway: Restriction endonucleases recognize specific DNA sequences and cleave the DNA internally at or near those sites.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q001.displayText:
Restriction endonucleases recognize specific DNA sequences and cleave the DNA internally at or near those sites.

Enzymes that cut DNA at specific DNA sequences within the molecule are called restriction
enzymes. eC,"
These defensive enzymes protect the host bacterial DNA from the DNA genome ‘of foreign
organisms (primarily infective phages) by specifically inactivating the invading phage DNA by
digestion. — ~"
emphasis: Restriction endonucleases recognize specific DNA sequences and cleave the DNA internally at or near those sites

rationales.a: Helicase separates DNA strands during replication but does not make sequence-specific internal cuts.
rationales.b: DNA polymerase synthesizes DNA from a template rather than cleaving it at recognition sequences.
rationales.d: Gyrase is a bacterial topoisomerase that changes DNA supercoiling; restriction enzymes perform site-specific cleavage.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q005.takeaway: Molecular cloning vectors include plasmids and bacteriophages (as well as cosmids) to propagate recombinant DNA.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q005.displayText:
Molecular cloning vectors include plasmids and bacteriophages (as well as cosmids) to propagate recombinant DNA.

Gene cloning uses both plasmids and bacteriophages.
Hybrid DNA molecules can be constructed in cloning vectors typically using bacterial plasmids,
phages, or cosmids. A clone is a large population of identical molecules, bacteria, or cells that
arise from a common ancestor. Molecular cloning allows for the production of a large number of
identical DNA molecules, which can then be characterized or used for other purposes.
emphasis: Molecular cloning vectors include plasmids and bacteriophages (as well as cosmids) to propagate recombinant DNA

rationales.a: Plasmids are cloning vectors, but this single option omits bacteriophages, which are also used.
rationales.b: A noncoding sequence alone is not a vector; cloning uses a replicating carrier such as a plasmid or phage.
rationales.c: Bacteriophages are cloning vectors, but this single option omits plasmids, which are also used.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q010.takeaway: Ideal PCR doubles target DNA each cycle; 30 cycles yield about 2³⁰, or 10⁹, copies from one template.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q010.displayText:
Ideal PCR doubles target DNA each cycle; 30 cycles yield about 2³⁰, or 10⁹, copies from one template.

A PCR reaction that continues for 30 cycles will produce approximately 1 billion PCR products
from a single template DNA molecule.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a method of amplifying a target sequence of DNA. DNA
sequences as short as 50 to 100 bp and as long as 10 kb can be amplified by PCR. The
amplification is exponential.
* 20 cycles provide amplification of 220 = 106 or 1 million copies
* 30 cycles provide an amplification of 230 =109 or 1 billion copies
emphasis: Ideal PCR doubles target DNA each cycle; 30 cycles yield about 2³⁰, or 10⁹, copies from one template

rationales.a: 64 copies corresponds to only about six ideal doublings, far fewer than 30 cycles.
rationales.b: 128,000 is far below the ideal 2³⁰ amplification expected after 30 cycles.
rationales.c: About one million copies corresponds roughly to 20 cycles, not 30.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q014.takeaway: PCR amplification of short tandem-repeat loci is central to DNA profiling for forensic identification and paternity analysis.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q014.displayText:
PCR amplification of short tandem-repeat loci is central to DNA profiling for forensic identification and paternity analysis.

PCR is used for DNA profiling (DNA fingerprinting).
The PCR allows the DNA in a single cell, hair follicle, or spermatozoon to be amplified and
analyzed. Thus, the applications of PCR to forensic medicine are obvious. DNA fingerprinting, or
DNA profiling, is used for forensic analysis of crime scenes and paternity testing (Option D).
Other options:
Option A: Short Tandem Repeat (STR) are short sequences of DNA at scattered locations in the
genome, repeated in tandem (one after the other). E.g., CG-CG-CG-CG-CG. The number of these
repeat units varies from person to person but is unique for any given individual and, therefore,
serves as a molecular fingerprint.
Option B: Single Nucleotide Polymorphism(SNP) refers to variations that involve just one base at
a given locus (Eg., base C replaced by base A), which can occur within exons, introns, intergenic or
coding regions. They are almost always biallelic and are majorly used in the definition of inherited
diseases where the functional deficit is unknown. Each of these variations is present to some
appreciable degree within a population and hence not unique to an individual.
emphasis: PCR amplification of short tandem-repeat loci is central to DNA profiling for forensic identification and paternity analysis

rationales.a: STR profiles are highly discriminating but are not literally unique in every possible case, so this statement is false.
rationales.b: Forensic profiling chiefly uses noncoding STR loci, not SNPs specifically selected from coding sequences.
rationales.d: DNA profiling can be used in paternity testing as well as forensic casework.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q015.takeaway: Classical radioactive in situ hybridization localizes genes on metaphase chromosomes by probe hybridization and autoradiographic detection.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q015.displayText:
Classical radioactive in situ hybridization localizes genes on metaphase chromosomes by probe hybridization and autoradiographic detection.

In situ hybridization uses a radioactive probe for gene localization.
It is added to a metaphase spread of chromosomes on a glass slide. The exact area of
hybridization is localized by layering photographic emulsion over the slide and after exposure,
lining up the grains with some histologic identification of the chromosome.
Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) utilizes fluorescent probes, not radioactive probes.
Fluorescent probes have greater safety, stability, and ease of detection (Option C).
emphasis: Classical radioactive in situ hybridization localizes genes on metaphase chromosomes by probe hybridization and autoradiographic detection

rationales.a: Somatic-cell hybridization maps genes by retention patterns in hybrid cell lines rather than by radioactive probe localization on chromosomes.
rationales.c: FISH uses fluorescently labeled probes and fluorescent microscopy rather than a radioactive probe.
rationales.d: Because FISH uses fluorescence and somatic-cell hybridization uses cell-line mapping, not all listed methods use radioactive probes.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q017.takeaway: RFLPs can support linkage mapping, QTL mapping and diagnosis of single-gene variants when a polymorphism tracks the disease allele.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q017.displayText:
RFLPs can support linkage mapping, QTL mapping and diagnosis of single-gene variants when a polymorphism tracks the disease allele.

© we
Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) is used to construct a high-resolution linkage
map, QTL mapsyand identify single gene-disease.
An inherited difference in the’pattern of restriction enzyme digestion (e.g., a DNA variation
occurring in more than 1% of the general population) is known as a restriction fragment length
polymorphism (RFLP). RFLPs result from single-base changes (e.g., sickle-cell disease) or from
deletions or insertions (CNVs) of DNA into a restriction fragment (eg, the thalassemias) and have
proved to be useful diagnostic tools.
SNPs(single nucleotide polymorphisms)/RFLPs can be used to establish linkage groups, which in
turn, by the process of chromosome walking, will eventually define the disease locus.
emphasis: RFLPs can support linkage mapping, QTL mapping and diagnosis of single-gene variants when a polymorphism tracks the disease allele

rationales.a: Restriction-fragment polymorphisms can serve as markers in high-resolution linkage maps.
rationales.b: RFLP markers can track a disease locus in families, supporting analysis of single-gene disorders.
rationales.c: RFLP markers can be used to construct quantitative-trait-locus maps, so all listed applications apply.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q018.takeaway: CRISPR-Cas9 originated as bacterial adaptive immunity: guide RNA directs Cas nucleases to complementary invading DNA.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q018.displayText:
CRISPR-Cas9 originated as bacterial adaptive immunity: guide RNA directs Cas nucleases to complementary invading DNA.

The CRISPR-Cas9 system, found in many bacteria, represents a form of acquired, or adaptive
immunity to infection by bacteriophages, which complements the system of restriction
endonucleases and methylases.
In recent years, a novel DNA editing/gene regulatory system termed Clustered Regularly
Interspersed Short Palindromic Repeats- CRISPR-associated gene 9 (CRISPR-Cas9) has been
developed. CRISPR uses RNA-based targeting to bring the Cas9 nuclease to foreign (or any
complementary) DNA.
Within bacteria, this CRISPR-RNA-Cas9 complex then degrades and inactivates the targeted
DNA.
emphasis: CRISPR-Cas9 originated as bacterial adaptive immunity: guide RNA directs Cas nucleases to complementary invading DNA

rationales.b: CRISPR-Cas systems are not inherently a tuberculosis diagnostic test; they are microbial defense systems adapted for biotechnology.
rationales.c: The system is a nucleic-acid targeting mechanism, not a tool designed to test air pollution.
rationales.d: CRISPR can be used in molecular applications, but its biological role is not DNA sequencing; bacteria use it as adaptive immunity.
